title: Directing solvent reactivity - Nature Energy
gist: A short News & Views commentary by Sanghyun Park and Yong-Mook Kang of Korea University on the DOX electrolyte work. It argues that a low-strain cyclic solvent forming an oligomerized interphase enables highly reversible sodium deposition in anode-free sodium batteries without additives or electrode modifications. Only the teaser paragraph is available; the full text is paywalled.

insights.claim: Anode-free sodium batteries maximize cell-level energy density because they remove the excess sodium on the anode, but irreversible sodium loss during plating and stripping limits them.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Energy-density gains depend on solving sodium loss.
insights.quote: eliminate excessive sodium on the anode, maximizing cell-level energy density

insights.claim: A low-strain cyclic solvent can form an oligomerized interphase that enables highly reversible sodium deposition without functional additives or electrode modifications.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Removing the need for additives and electrode changes simplifies manufacturing and cuts cost for sodium-metal cells.
insights.quote: enabling highly reversible sodium deposition without functional additives or electrode modifications

insights.claim: The commentary frames the advance as directing solvent reactivity: the 1,3-dioxane (DOX) solvent molecule itself regulates both solvation and interphase formation, so electrolyte decomposition becomes a design tool instead of a failure mode.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: This shifts electrolyte R&D toward choosing solvent molecules by reactivity, not just stability.

insights.claim: Independent experts at Korea University (Sanghyun Park and Yong-Mook Kang) highlighted the DOX anode-free sodium battery study by Ding et al. in Nature Energy, which signals the field sees it as notable.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Editorial highlighting raises the odds the approach is taken up by other groups and industry.
